questions.question: Which set of evaluation criteria is most appropriate when comparing two blind search algorithms such as truth‑table enumeration and depth‑first model enumeration?

options.A: Only time complexity, because space is negligible for propositional problems.
options.B: Completeness, time complexity, and space complexity, because these affect whether the algorithm finds a solution and its resource usage.
options.C: Optimality and heuristic quality, since both algorithms use heuristics to guide the search.
options.D: Number of logical inference rules applied, as this determines soundness.

questions.explanation:
The text emphasizes comparing algorithms by “time and space complexity” and mentions completeness (e.g., “depth‑first enumeration of all models is sound and complete”) – standard criteria for evaluating search methods. [Page 184‑185]

---

questions.question: How do the space requirements of truth‑table enumeration and depth‑first model enumeration compare?

options.A: Both require exponential space because they must store all possible assignments simultaneously.
options.B: Truth‑table enumeration requires exponential space, while depth‑first model enumeration can be performed with linear space in the number of symbols.
options.C: Truth‑table enumeration uses linear space, whereas depth‑first model enumeration needs exponential space due to recursion depth.
options.D: Both use only constant extra space because they generate assignments on the fly.

questions.explanation:
The context states “O(2ⁿ) for n symbols” for truth‑table enumeration, implying exponential space, while depth‑first enumeration can reuse a single path, needing only O(n) space. [Page 184‑185]

questions.question: According to the provided material, which blind search method is guaranteed to find a solution if one exists in a finite propositional search space?

options.D: Uninformed backtracking that stops after the first failure.

questions.explanation:
The passage notes that “depth‑first enumeration of all models is sound and complete,” meaning it will find a solution when one exists in a finite space. [Page 184‑185]

questions.question: When comparing improved backtracking (e.g., DPLL) with heuristic search in model space (e.g., min‑conflicts hill‑climbing), which statement correctly reflects their trade‑offs?

options.A: Both methods are complete, but backtracking has higher time complexity than heuristic search.
options.B: Backtracking is sound and complete but may explore many branches; heuristic search is sound but incomplete, often faster on large instances.
options.C: Heuristic search always yields optimal solutions, whereas backtracking does not guarantee optimality.
options.D: Backtracking uses a heuristic to prune the search tree, while hill‑climbing enumerates all possible models.

questions.explanation:
The context describes “improved backtracking… sound but incomplete” for model‑space heuristics, and notes that “min‑conflicts‑like hill‑climbing algorithms” are heuristic and thus not guaranteed to find a solution, though they can be faster. [Page 185]

questions.question: In the context of logical inference, which of the following best evaluates the difference between forward chaining and backward chaining?

options.A: Forward chaining is goal‑directed and therefore generates fewer inferences than backward chaining.
options.B: Backward chaining starts from the query and only expands relevant rules, often reducing the number of generated sentences compared with forward chaining.
options.C: Both chaining methods always explore the entire knowledge base, so their efficiency is identical.
options.D: Backward chaining cannot be expressed as a search algorithm, while forward chaining can.

questions.explanation: The text presents backward chaining as a “goal‑directed” search that unifies with goals, implying it expands only necessary parts of the KB, unlike forward chaining which indiscriminately applies all rules. [Page 209]
